By the 1770s the Winterodes had come north over the Maryland line into the rolling farm country of York County,
Pennsylvania, the part that became Adams County in 1800.
In 1779 Jacob Winteroth bought a hundred acres in Germany Township, by Littlestown,
and in 1783 he was taxed on 150 acres with ten people in the house.
It was Pennsylvania German country, Lutheran and Reformed, where the families built their own churches:
Christ Reformed in Union Township, where the Winterodes are buried, and Mark's Reformed,
which Andreas Eschbach helped found in 1789.
In the Revolution Jacob, by a county historian's account, served as an ensign, and a Johann Adam Wintroth,
thought to be his brother, was lieutenant colonel of the 7th Battalion of York County militia.
For four generations the family farmed and married its neighbours, the Eschbachs,
the Winebrenners of Hanover, the Pollys and Ogdens of Gettysburg, and stayed.
Then, in July 1863, the war came to their fields.
Francis Ogden had sowed the wheat on the farm that became the battle's Wheatfield,
moving off that spring, and Edward Wintrode rode with a cavalry company raised in the county.
South of town the Emmitsburg Road crosses a rise that battlefield guides still call Wintrode Ridge,
near where Edward’s father Samuel was farming in 1860; Confederate guns held it on 3 July,
and Union cavalry fought up the road toward it after Pickett’s Charge.
A few years after the war the family went west.
